Cerebrovascular.title: Cerebrovascular System
Cerebrovascular.quickSummary: The cerebrovascular system includes the carotid and vertebral arteries that supply blood to the brain. Understanding their anatomy, flow patterns, and pathology is critical for stroke prevention.
keyPoints: Common carotid artery bifurcates into internal and external carotid arteries
ICA supplies the brain (no branches in neck), ECA supplies face/scalp (has branches)
Normal ICA waveform: low resistance with forward diastolic flow
Normal ECA waveform: high resistance with oscillating flow
Vertebral arteries arise from subclavian arteries and join to form basilar artery
Circle of Willis provides collateral circulation to the brain
clinicalPearls: ICA stenosis ≥70% is significant and may require intervention
Spectral broadening indicates turbulent flow and possible stenosis
Plaque morphology matters: heterogeneous plaque is higher risk than homogeneous
Always check for vertebral artery reversal (subclavian steal syndrome)
Post-stenotic turbulence appears as color aliasing and mosaic pattern
The bulb is the most common location for atherosclerotic plaque

anatomy.title: Carotid Anatomy
anatomy.content:
**Common Carotid Artery (CCA)**
• Right CCA: branches from brachiocephalic trunk
• Left CCA: branches directly from aortic arch
• Bifurcates at C3-C5 level into ICA and ECA

**Internal Carotid Artery (ICA)**
• Supplies the brain
• Larger diameter than ECA
• No extracranial branches
• Low resistance flow pattern
• Has a bulb at origin (dilated segment)

**External Carotid Artery (ECA)**
• Supplies face, scalp, and neck
• Smaller diameter than ICA
• Has multiple branches (superior thyroid, lingual, facial)
• High resistance flow pattern
• Can tap to identify (temporal tap test)

**Vertebral Arteries**
• Arise from subclavian arteries
• Enter transverse foramina at C6
• Join to form basilar artery
• Part of posterior circulation

hemodynamics.title: Flow Patterns
hemodynamics.content:
**Normal ICA Waveform**
• Low resistance pattern
• Forward flow throughout cardiac cycle
• Broad systolic peak
• Significant diastolic flow
• PSV typically 60-100 cm/s
• No flow reversal

**Normal ECA Waveform**
• High resistance pattern
• Sharp systolic peak
• Minimal or reversed diastolic flow
• May see oscillating flow
• Responds to temporal tap

**Normal CCA Waveform**
• Mixed pattern (combination of ICA and ECA)
• Moderate diastolic flow
• PSV typically 50-80 cm/s

pathology.title: Common Pathology
pathology.content:
**Carotid Stenosis**
• <50%: PSV <125 cm/s, no intervention needed
• 50-69%: PSV 125-230 cm/s, medical management
• ≥70%: PSV >230 cm/s, ICA/CCA ratio >4.0, consider intervention
• Critical: PSV >400 cm/s, severe turbulence

**Plaque Characteristics**
• Homogeneous: uniform echogenicity, more stable
• Heterogeneous: mixed echoes, higher embolic risk
• Calcified: highly echogenic with shadowing
• Ulcerated: irregular surface, embolic source

**Other Pathology**
• Occlusion: no flow, may see stump
• Dissection: intimal flap, double lumen
• Aneurysm: focal dilation >50% normal diameter
• Fibromuscular dysplasia: string of beads appearance

protocols.title: Scanning Protocol
protocols.content:
**Standard Exam**
1. CCA proximal, mid, distal in long and transverse
2. Carotid bulb - multiple angles
3. ICA proximal, mid, distal
4. ECA origin
5. Vertebral arteries bilaterally

**Doppler Techniques**
• Angle of insonation: 60° or less
• Sample volume: 1.5-2mm, centered in vessel
• Wall filter: low setting to see diastolic flow
• PRF: adjust to prevent aliasing
• Color gain: just below noise level

**Measurements**
• PSV (peak systolic velocity)
• EDV (end diastolic velocity)
• ICA/CCA ratio
• Diameter measurements in transverse
• Percent stenosis calculation

Arterial Hemodynamics.title: Arterial Hemodynamics
Arterial Hemodynamics.quickSummary: Arterial hemodynamics involves understanding blood flow patterns, velocity measurements, and waveform analysis to detect and quantify arterial disease.
keyPoints: Normal arterial waveform is triphasic: forward systole, reverse early diastole, forward late diastole
Biphasic waveform indicates mild disease - loss of reverse component
Monophasic waveform indicates significant disease - only forward flow
Peak Systolic Velocity (PSV) increases with stenosis severity
Post-stenotic turbulence appears as spectral broadening
Velocity ratios help quantify stenosis severity
clinicalPearls: PSV increase of 100% or velocity ratio >2.0 indicates ≥50% stenosis
Tardus parvus waveform suggests proximal stenosis or occlusion
Dampened waveform indicates downstream obstruction
Collateral flow is typically high resistance (like ECA pattern)
Always compare contralateral side for asymmetry
Calcification can cause velocity overestimation

waveforms.title: Waveform Analysis
waveforms.content:
**Triphasic Waveform (Normal)**
• Phase 1: Rapid systolic upstroke and peak
• Phase 2: Brief flow reversal in early diastole
• Phase 3: Small forward flow in late diastole
• Indicates normal, healthy artery
• Seen in upper extremities and proximal lower extremities

**Biphasic Waveform (Mild Disease)**
• Forward systolic flow
• Loss of reverse component
• Forward diastolic flow
• Suggests mild proximal disease
• Common in older patients or mild PAD

**Monophasic Waveform (Significant Disease)**
• Single forward flow component
• Rounded, dampened appearance
• Low velocity
• Indicates significant proximal disease
• Often seen distal to stenosis or occlusion

**Tardus Parvus**
• Delayed systolic upstroke (tardus = slow)
• Decreased amplitude (parvus = small)
• Indicates severe proximal stenosis
• Acceleration time >140ms is abnormal

velocities.title: Velocity Criteria
velocities.content:
**Normal Values**
• CFA: PSV 80-120 cm/s
• SFA: PSV 70-110 cm/s
• Popliteal: PSV 60-90 cm/s
• Tibial: PSV 40-60 cm/s

**Stenosis Criteria**
• <50% stenosis: PSV <2x proximal
• 50-75% stenosis: PSV 2-4x proximal, spectral broadening
• >75% stenosis: PSV >4x proximal, aliasing, post-stenotic turbulence
• Critical stenosis: PSV >400 cm/s or severe dampening

**Velocity Ratios**
• Stenotic PSV / Proximal PSV >2.0 = ≥50% stenosis
• Stenotic PSV / Proximal PSV >3.5 = ≥75% stenosis
• Used to normalize for cardiac output variations

resistance.title: Resistance Patterns
resistance.content:
**High Resistance (Peripheral)**
• Supplies muscle at rest
• Minimal diastolic flow
• May see flow reversal
• Example: ECA, resting limb arteries

**Low Resistance (Cerebral/Visceral)**
• Supplies organs needing constant flow
• Continuous forward diastolic flow
• No flow reversal
• Example: ICA, renal, mesenteric

**Resistance Indices**
• Resistive Index (RI) = (PSV-EDV)/PSV
  - Normal: 0.6-0.8
  - High: >0.8
  - Low: <0.6
• Pulsatility Index (PI) = (PSV-EDV)/mean velocity

Arterial Anatomy.title: Arterial Anatomy
Arterial Anatomy.quickSummary: Understanding arterial anatomy is fundamental to performing accurate vascular ultrasound examinations and identifying pathology.
keyPoints: Aorta branches into common iliac arteries at L4 level
External iliac becomes common femoral artery (CFA) at inguinal ligament
CFA bifurcates into superficial femoral artery (SFA) and profunda femoris
SFA becomes popliteal artery at adductor hiatus
Popliteal trifurcates into anterior tibial, posterior tibial, and peroneal arteries
Upper extremity: subclavian → axillary → brachial → radial/ulnar
clinicalPearls: The SFA is NOT superficial - it's a deep artery despite the name
Profunda femoris is the main blood supply to the thigh, not the SFA
Adductor hiatus is where SFA transitions to popliteal - key landmark
Anterior tibial crosses interosseous membrane to anterior compartment
Posterior tibial and peroneal stay in posterior compartment
Palmar arch in hand and plantar arch in foot provide collateral circulation

lowerExtremity.title: Lower Extremity Arteries
lowerExtremity.content:
**Aorta and Iliac System**
• Abdominal aorta bifurcates at L4 into common iliac arteries
• Common iliac → Internal iliac (supplies pelvis) and External iliac
• External iliac becomes CFA at inguinal ligament

**Femoral Arteries**
• Common Femoral Artery (CFA)
  - Palpable at inguinal ligament
  - Bifurcates ~4cm below inguinal ligament
  - Bifurcation into SFA and profunda femoris

• Superficial Femoral Artery (SFA)
  - Continues down medial thigh
  - Travels through adductor (Hunter's) canal
  - Most common site of atherosclerosis in leg
  - Becomes popliteal at adductor hiatus

• Profunda Femoris (Deep Femoral)
  - Supplies thigh musculature
  - Main collateral source if SFA is occluded
  - Usually dives deep and difficult to follow

**Popliteal Artery**
• Continuation of SFA at adductor hiatus
• Runs behind knee in popliteal fossa
• Trifurcates below knee into 3 vessels

**Tibial Arteries**
• Anterior Tibial (AT)
  - Crosses interosseous membrane
  - Runs in anterior compartment
  - Becomes dorsalis pedis at ankle

• Posterior Tibial (PT)
  - Stays in posterior compartment
  - Palpable behind medial malleolus
  - Supplies plantar arch

• Peroneal (Fibular)
  - Stays in posterior compartment
  - Runs along fibula
  - Often dominant vessel in disease

upperExtremity.title: Upper Extremity Arteries
upperExtremity.content:
**Aortic Arch Branches**
• Brachiocephalic (innominate)
  - First branch of aortic arch
  - Divides into right CCA and right subclavian
• Left Common Carotid (second branch)
• Left Subclavian (third branch)

**Subclavian Artery**
• Extends from aortic arch to lateral border of first rib
• Gives off vertebral artery
• Becomes axillary artery

**Axillary Artery**
• From first rib to lower border of teres major
• Divided into 3 segments by pectoralis minor
• Becomes brachial artery

**Brachial Artery**
• Main artery of upper arm
• Bifurcates at antecubital fossa
• Divides into radial and ulnar arteries

**Radial and Ulnar Arteries**
• Radial: lateral forearm, palpable at wrist
• Ulnar: medial forearm, larger of the two
• Join to form superficial and deep palmar arches
• Palmar arches supply hand and fingers

collaterals.title: Collateral Pathways
collaterals.content:
**Lower Extremity Collaterals**
• Profunda femoris branches → Genicular branches
• Internal iliac → External iliac bypass
• Circumflex arteries around hip
• Genicular arteries around knee

**Upper Extremity Collaterals**
• Subscapular branches
• Circumflex humeral arteries
• Collateral arteries around elbow

**Significance**
• Allow blood flow despite stenosis or occlusion
• Usually smaller, more tortuous vessels
• Can remodel and enlarge over time
• Important for symptom development

Arterial Disease.title: Arterial Disease
Arterial Disease.quickSummary: Arterial disease encompasses atherosclerosis, aneurysms, dissections, and other vascular pathologies that can lead to ischemia, stroke, or rupture.
keyPoints: Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) affects 8-12% of population
Atherosclerosis is the most common arterial disease
Aneurysm = vessel dilation >50% normal diameter
AAA >5.5cm requires surgical intervention
Claudication indicates arterial insufficiency with exercise
Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) is key screening tool for PAD
clinicalPearls: PAD risk factors: smoking, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia
Critical limb ischemia = rest pain, ulcers, gangrene - needs urgent treatment
Aneurysm rupture risk increases with size and growth rate
Aortic dissection is a surgical emergency - look for intimal flap
Acute limb ischemia = 6 P's: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paresthesia, Paralysis, Poikilothermia
Diabetic patients may have calcified vessels affecting ABI accuracy

atherosclerosis.title: Atherosclerotic Disease
atherosclerosis.content:
**Pathophysiology**
• Plaque buildup in arterial walls
• Narrows lumen → reduced blood flow
• Can rupture → thrombosis, embolism
• Progressive disease over decades

**Risk Factors**
• Smoking (most important modifiable risk)
• Diabetes mellitus
• Hypertension
• Hyperlipidemia
• Age (>65 years)
• Family history
• Chronic kidney disease

**Clinical Presentation**
• Asymptomatic (early disease)
• Intermittent claudication
  - Calf pain with walking
  - Relieved by rest
  - Reproducible distance
• Rest pain (advanced disease)
• Tissue loss (critical limb ischemia)

**Ultrasound Findings**
• Intimal thickening
• Plaque (echogenic material)
• Stenosis (narrowing)
• Increased velocities
• Post-stenotic turbulence
• Dampened distal waveforms

**Stenosis Grading**
• <50%: minimal hemodynamic significance
• 50-75%: moderate stenosis
• >75%: severe stenosis, hemodynamically significant
• Occlusion: no flow, may see collaterals

aneurysm.title: Aneurysmal Disease
aneurysm.content:
**Definition**
• Permanent dilation >50% normal diameter
• True aneurysm: involves all 3 vessel layers
• Pseudoaneurysm: contained rupture

**Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA)**
• Normal aorta: <3cm diameter
• Aneurysm: ≥3cm diameter
• Screening recommended: men >65 who ever smoked
• Intervention criteria:
  - ≥5.5cm diameter
  - Growth >0.5cm in 6 months
  - Symptomatic
  - Rupture risk: 25-40% at 5.5cm

**Popliteal Aneurysm**
• Most common peripheral aneurysm
• Normal popliteal: <1cm
• Aneurysm: ≥2cm (or >1.5cm + 50% larger than contralateral)
• Risk: thrombosis and distal embolization
• Often bilateral (50-70%)

**Femoral Artery Aneurysm**
• Less common
• Often associated with AAA
• Usually true aneurysms

**Pseudoaneurysm**
• Iatrogenic (post-catheterization most common)
• Contained rupture with fibrous capsule
• Shows swirling "yin-yang" color flow
• To-and-fro waveform in neck
• Treatment: compression, thrombin injection, surgery

other.title: Other Arterial Pathology
other.content:
**Aortic Dissection**
• Tear in intimal layer
• Blood enters vessel wall creating false lumen
• Stanford Type A: involves ascending aorta (surgical emergency)
• Stanford Type B: descending aorta only (medical management)
• Ultrasound: intimal flap, dual lumens

**Thrombosis**
• Acute: sudden onset ischemia, 6 P's
• Chronic: gradual onset, collaterals develop
• Ultrasound: echogenic material filling lumen, no flow

**Embolism**
• From proximal source (heart, aneurysm, plaque)
• Lodges at arterial bifurcations
• Sudden onset symptoms
• "Blue toe syndrome" from microemboli

**Arteritis**
• Takayasu arteritis: large vessel inflammation
• Giant cell arteritis: temporal arteries, age >50
• Ultrasound: wall thickening (halo sign)

**Fibromuscular Dysplasia (FMD)**
• Non-atherosclerotic arterial disease
• "String of beads" appearance
• Most common in renal and carotid arteries
• Typically young women

**Compartment Syndrome**
• Increased pressure in closed muscle compartment
• Can compromise arterial flow
• Surgical emergency if severe

Venous Hemodynamics.title: Venous Hemodynamics
Venous Hemodynamics.quickSummary: Venous hemodynamics involves understanding venous flow patterns, valve function, and the dynamics that promote or impair venous return.
keyPoints: Normal venous flow is phasic with respiration (spontaneous)
Augmentation increases flow when distal limb is compressed
Competent valves close in <0.5 seconds after release
Reflux >0.5 seconds (CFV) or >1.0 seconds (other veins) indicates valve incompetence
Valsalva normally causes flow cessation in competent veins
Loss of respiratory phasicity suggests proximal obstruction
clinicalPearls: Augmentation tests valve competence - squeeze calf and watch for reflux
Phasicity confirms patency - if present, no occlusion proximal
Post-thrombotic syndrome from valve damage after DVT
Chronic venous insufficiency can lead to ulceration
Perforator incompetence causes superficial varicosities
Always examine patient in reverse Trendelenburg or standing for reflux

flowPatterns.title: Normal Venous Flow
flowPatterns.content:
**Characteristics of Normal Venous Flow**
• Spontaneous: flow present without augmentation
• Phasic: varies with respiration
  - Inspiration: decreased or reversed (lower extremity)
  - Expiration: increased flow
  - Opposite in upper extremity and neck
• Augmentable: increases with distal compression
• Non-pulsatile: (unless right heart failure or tricuspid regurgitation)

**Respiratory Phasicity**
• Lower extremity veins:
  - Inspiration → increased intra-abdominal pressure → flow decreases
  - Expiration → decreased pressure → flow increases
• Upper extremity veins:
  - Opposite pattern
• Significance: confirms patency to central veins

**Augmentation Response**
• Distal compression → increased venous return
• Tests patency between compression site and probe
• Brisk augmentation with normal veins
• Blunted or absent with obstruction
• Used to locate occlusions

valves.title: Venous Valve Function
valves.content:
**Normal Valve Function**
• Prevent retrograde flow (reflux)
• Unidirectional flow toward heart
• Close during reversed pressure gradient
• Found throughout deep and superficial veins
• More numerous in distal leg veins

**Valve Closure Time**
• Normal: <0.5 seconds (common femoral vein)
• Normal: <1.0 seconds (other deep veins)
• Abnormal reflux: longer than these values
• Indicates valve incompetence

**Testing Valve Competence**
• Patient positioning: reverse Trendelenburg or standing
• Valsalva maneuver:
  - Competent: flow stops or minimal reflux <0.5s
  - Incompetent: sustained reflux >0.5s
• Proximal compression and release:
  - Watch for reflux duration
• Distal augmentation:
  - Quick release → watch for reflux

**Reflux Grading**
• Grade 1: reflux to thigh
• Grade 2: reflux to knee
• Grade 3: reflux to calf
• Grade 4: reflux to ankle

pathology.title: Venous Pathology
pathology.content:
**Deep Venous Thrombosis (DVT)**
• Acute: non-compressible vein, echogenic thrombus
• Chronic: partial compressibility, recanalization
• Flow: absent or reduced
• No augmentation response
• No respiratory phasicity if proximal obstruction

**Chronic Venous Insufficiency (CVI)**
• Result of valve incompetence
• Causes: post-thrombotic syndrome, primary valve failure
• Reflux >1.0 second on Doppler
• Clinical: edema, skin changes, ulcers
• Often involves perforator veins

**Superficial Venous Reflux**
• Great saphenous vein (GSV) incompetence
• Small saphenous vein (SSV) incompetence  
• Perforator incompetence
• Causes varicose veins
• Can lead to symptoms without DVT

**May-Thurner Syndrome**
• Left common iliac vein compressed by right common iliac artery
• Can cause left leg swelling and DVT
• More common in women

**Superior Vena Cava (SVC) Syndrome**
• Obstruction of SVC
• Causes: tumor, catheter thrombosis
• Symptoms: face/arm swelling, collateral veins

techniques.title: Examination Techniques
techniques.content:
**Compression Ultrasound**
• Primary method for DVT detection
• Complete compression = patent vein
• Non-compressible = thrombosis
• Assess every 1-2cm along vein length

**Doppler Assessment**
• Spontaneity: is flow present?
• Phasicity: does it vary with respiration?
• Augmentation: increases with compression?
• Valsalva response: does flow stop?

**Color Doppler**
• Confirms flow presence
• Shows flow direction
• Identifies reflux
• Detects collateral veins

**Reflux Testing**
• Patient position: standing or reverse Trendelenburg
• Use automatic cuff or manual compression
• Measure reflux duration
• Document worst reflux time

General & Other.title: General Vascular & Other Topics
General & Other.quickSummary: Covers physics principles, instrumentation, scanning protocols, patient care, and other essential knowledge for vascular sonography.
keyPoints: Doppler shift = 2 × velocity × frequency × cos(θ) / propagation speed
Angle of insonation should be ≤60° for accurate velocity measurements
Higher frequency probes give better resolution but less penetration
Color Doppler shows flow direction and presence of flow
Spectral Doppler provides velocity information
Always use standardized protocols for consistency
clinicalPearls: Never exceed 60° angle - velocities become inaccurate
Use lowest frequency that gives adequate image for better penetration
Color aliasing indicates high velocities - suggests stenosis
Keep PRF (pulse repetition frequency) as low as possible without aliasing
Wall filter set too high can eliminate important low-velocity flow
Document protocol: images, measurements, and interpretation

physics.title: Ultrasound Physics
physics.content:
**Doppler Principles**
• Doppler Effect: frequency shift when waves reflect from moving objects
• Positive shift: flow toward transducer
• Negative shift: flow away from transducer
• Doppler Equation: Δf = 2 × v × f₀ × cos(θ) / c
  - Δf = frequency shift
  - v = blood velocity
  - f₀ = transmitted frequency
  - θ = angle of insonation
  - c = speed of sound (1540 m/s in soft tissue)

**Angle of Insonation**
• Critical for accurate velocity measurement
• Should be ≤60° (preferably 45-60°)
• At 90°: cos(90°) = 0, no Doppler shift
• At 0°: cos(0°) = 1, maximum Doppler shift
• Angle correction must be parallel to vessel wall

**Frequency vs Resolution**
• Higher frequency → better resolution, less penetration
• Lower frequency → worse resolution, better penetration
• Carotid: 5-10 MHz linear probe
• Peripheral arteries: 5-10 MHz linear
• Abdominal vessels: 2-5 MHz curved/phased array

**Aliasing**
• Occurs when velocities exceed Nyquist limit
• Nyquist limit = PRF / 2
• Appears as color reversal or spectral wraparound
• Solutions:
  - Increase PRF
  - Decrease frequency
  - Increase angle
  - Use continuous wave Doppler

instrumentation.title: Instrumentation & Controls
instrumentation.content:
**Color Doppler Controls**
• Color Gain: adjust to just below noise
• Color Box: keep small for better frame rate
• PRF (Scale): set to show flow without aliasing
• Wall Filter: remove low-frequency noise (vessel wall motion)
• Baseline: shift up/down to show faster flow

**Spectral Doppler Controls**
• Sample Volume (Gate): 1.5-2mm, centered in vessel
• Angle Correction: align with flow direction
• Sweep Speed: faster for arterial, slower for venous
• Gain: adjust to see waveform without noise
• PRF: prevent aliasing while keeping scale appropriate
• Wall Filter: low for venous, moderate for arterial
• Invert: flip spectrum if needed for display

**Optimization Tips**
• 2D Image:
  - Depth: only as deep as needed
  - Focus: at level of interest
  - Gain: optimize gray scale
  - TGC: even brightness throughout image
• Doppler:
  - Angle ≤60°
  - Sample volume in center of vessel
  - Gain to see waveform clearly
  - PRF to prevent aliasing

protocols.title: Standard Protocols
protocols.content:
**Carotid Artery Protocol**
1. CCA: proximal, mid, distal (long/trans)
2. Bulb: multiple angles
3. ICA: proximal, mid, distal
4. ECA: origin
5. Vertebral: origin, mid, distal bilaterally
6. Spectral Doppler: PSV, EDV, ICA/CCA ratio

**Lower Extremity Arterial**
1. CFA: spectral Doppler
2. Proximal, mid, distal SFA
3. Popliteal artery
4. Tibial arteries (AT, PT, peroneal) if needed
5. Document velocities and waveforms
6. Note stenosis locations and severity

**Lower Extremity Venous**
1. CFV: with and without compression
2. Femoral vein: scan entire length
3. Popliteal vein: behind knee
4. Posterior tibial and peroneal veins if needed
5. GSV if reflux study
6. Compression every 1-2cm
7. Augmentation and phasicity assessment

**Upper Extremity Arterial**
1. Subclavian: proximal and distal
2. Axillary artery
3. Brachial artery
4. Radial and ulnar arteries
5. Include blood pressure measurements
6. Document waveforms and velocities

**Abdominal Aorta**
1. Proximal aorta below diaphragm
2. Measure AP diameter in transverse (outer to outer)
3. Mid aorta
4. Distal aorta at bifurcation
5. Proximal common iliac arteries
6. Document maximum diameter

patientCare.title: Patient Care & Safety
patientCare.content:
**Patient Preparation**
• Carotid: no special prep, remove jewelry
• Abdominal aorta: NPO 6-8 hours (reduce bowel gas)
• Peripheral: comfortable positioning
• Venous: standing or reverse Trendelenburg for reflux

**During Exam**
• Explain procedure to patient
• Ensure privacy and comfort
• Use adequate gel
• Avoid excessive pressure (especially on carotids)
• Watch for patient discomfort
• Be aware of latex allergies

**Safety Considerations**
• ALARA principle (As Low As Reasonably Achievable)
• Minimize Doppler output power
• Minimize scan time
• Thermal Index (TI) and Mechanical Index (MI)
• Special care with carotid scanning (avoid reflex)

**Infection Control**
• Hand hygiene before and after
• Clean transducer per protocol
• Use covers when needed
• Fresh gel for each patient
• Clean gel bottles regularly
